source.title: Representational Similarity Alignment of Figurative Language in Humans and Large Language Models
source.authors: Samhita Bollepally; Aurora Sloman-Moll; Takashi Yamauchi; Neeka Motamedrasa

record.file_problem: None; full paper and supplementary materials are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures human–LLM representational similarity and compares it across a model-size series, using RSA on sentence-rating distances. This is a conceptual test of scale-related alignment, not a reproduction of cross-model alignment across different architectures or modalities.
record.gate_note: The study also compares surface-level similarity (SLS) with RSA and reports category-specific variation. These findings bear on metric and input dependence. It does not test image–caption alignment, same-architecture seed convergence, mapping/stitching, or recurring features. Prompt instructions were varied, but only reported aggregate correlations are recorded for the two prompt studies. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study does not test the claim; it measures a related but different construct. Its 'representations' are RDMs built from Likert ratings that humans and LLMs gave on 40 questions. They are behavioural output structures, not models' internal representations. The comparison is always human vs. model, never between independently trained models, between vision and language models, across seeds, by mapping, or by shared features. The Gemma size series (9B/27B/31B) relates human–model rating-structure alignment to size, not model–model representational convergence. The SLS-vs-RSA contrast likewise concerns human–model output agreement, not how a model–model convergence measure depends on its settings. The findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also stress that GPT-4 is closest to humans but still short of human–human consistency. They state that representational similarity patterns are independent of model size. Their RSA is computed on rating vectors, not on internal activations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RSA on human and LLM ratings of figurative-language sentences and a Gemma size series; it does not measure alignment between independently trained neural networks’ internal representations as in the original Platonic claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity measure (SLS versus RSA); sentence category and sensible versus non-sensible inputs; prompt wording/instructions (Study 1 versus Study 2).

fits_no_version.finding: Human–LLM alignment of rating-derived sentence RDMs is incomplete. Overall RSA is 0.19–0.65 (Table 3b) against human split-half RSA of .75–1.00, and is weakest for idiom, sarcasm and Gen Z slang.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs' behavioural similarity structure over figurative sentences only partially matches humans'.

fits_no_version.finding: Across Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-3-27B and Gemma-4-31B, human–model rating-structure alignment shows no consistent increase with size. Sarcasm and slang gains coexist with an emotional decline (.70 to .31).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human–model behavioural representational alignment does not reliably rise with model size within one family.

fits_no_version.finding: Output-level agreement (SLS) with humans exceeds rating-structure alignment (RSA) for most models, and alignment shifts with prompt wording. Llama's RSA falls from 0.49 to 0.19.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human–model alignment judged from outputs depends on the measure (SLS vs. RSA) and on the prompt.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says behavioral data are available on the authors’ GitHub Profile but provides no URL.
record.problems: The study uses 240 sentences constructed by the authors, with many items curated online, and 211 undergraduate human participants who reported English as their primary language. The authors note that the dataset is limited and constructed partly from their intuitions, sentences lack additional discourse context, and the selected models are only a subset of LLM families. The scale series is restricted to Gemma and the paper does not report a consistent size trend; several numerical results are ranges without model-specific assignments.
record.rows_left_out: No separately extractable per-category values were available in the figures as text for the general Study 1/2 model comparisons; figure-only category bars were not transcribed. The selected rows preserve the aggregate correlations in Table 3 and the explicitly stated Gemma-series values and ranges.

untested.parts: All of it: no model–model internal-representation alignment, and only human–model rating structure vs. Gemma size.
All of it: no vision models or image–caption pairs.
All of it: no seed replicates.
All of it: no mapping, stitching or relative representations.
All of it: no feature or circuit analysis.
All of it: SLS vs. RSA is compared for human–model output agreement, not for measured convergence between models.
All of it: incomplete human–model rating alignment is not model–model representational convergence; there is no plateau test and no shared-data analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V1, V6 and V7 labels are rejected. The study's 'representations' are RDMs of behavioural ratings compared to human ratings. None of its analyses concern convergence among models' internal representations, so all rows are relinked to none and no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model-size association within the Gemma series against human ratings, but does not test convergence among models with different architectures, objectives or data, and does not relate alignment to a measured capability change.
No vision and language models or paired images and captions.
No same-architecture models trained from different initializations or shared-feature/subspace analysis.
No mapping between models, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired alignment.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, circuits or SAE features.
Compares SLS and RSA and reports category-dependent outcomes, but does not vary RSA settings such as neighbour count or test out-of-distribution inputs.
Reports incomplete human–LLM representational alignment, but does not establish a plateau or test whether shared training data/objectives cause alignment rather than a common model of reality.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Gemma series across tested sizes and categories
reader_labels.reason: The authors report no consistent pattern of improvement across the Gemma size series; the reported emotional RSA range declines, despite category-specific gains for larger models. Rows R19–R27.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-3 to Gemma-4 on sensible sarcasm and Gen Z slang
reader_labels.reason: Reported RSA is higher for Gemma-4 than Gemma-3 in these categories, though this is category-specific and does not establish a general scale trend. Rows R20–R23.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Different similarity measures and sentence categories in the human–LLM comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The study reports different alignment patterns for SLS and RSA and variation by linguistic category, with conventional/emotional categories generally stronger than figurative categories. Rows R01–R16 and R19–R27.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Human–LLM representational similarity across the reported studies
reader_labels.reason: Model–human RSA is positive but incomplete, and the reported human–human RSA is higher; the authors describe persistent representational gaps. Rows R09–R18.
